patient_information: A 26-year-old Malawian woman. Her past medical history is reported as unremarkable. She lives in an urban high-density area and works as a businesswoman, selling vegetables. She has three healthy children, but four other children have died as toddlers. Her husband died a year ago of ‘high fever.’ An HIV test subsequently came back reactive.
chief_complaint: A 1-week history of headache, confusion for 2 days, and unilateral ptosis for 1 day.
history_of_present_illness: A 26-year-old Malawian woman has been unwell for at least 1 week. She complained of a headache of insidious onset and has been confused for 2 days. One day before presentation, her relatives noticed an eyelid drooping on the left side.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient lives in an urban high-density area in Malawi. Her husband died a year ago of 'high fever,' and four of her seven children have died as toddlers.
vitals: On examination, Glasgow Coma Scale was 14/15, temperature 38.4°C (101.1°F), blood pressure 115/75mmHg, heart rate 86bpm, and respiratory rate 18 breath cycles per minute.
physical_exam: She looks seriously unwell. There is no neck stiffness. The chest is clear. Examination of her eyes shows complete ptosis on the left. On primary gaze, the left eye is in a ‘down and out’ position, consistent with a third nerve palsy. The remainder of her neurological examination is normal.
labs_and_diagnostics: Blood results on admission (Table 3.1) showed WBC 3.2, Hb 10.2, and Platelets 124. Serum glucose was 4.0 mmol/L. A thick film for malaria and trypanosomes was negative. A lumbar puncture was done, revealing a markedly raised opening pressure at 32cmH2O. CSF results (Table 3.2) showed White cell count 28/μL, CSF protein 3.0 g/L, and CSF glucose 1.3 mmol/L. An HIV test came back reactive. India Ink stain, cryptococcal culture, and bacterial culture from the CSF were reported negative. Acid-fast bacilli were detected in the CSF (Fig. 3.2).
differential_diagnosis: The clinical syndrome was infectious meningitis. The differential diagnosis comprised bacterial, tuberculous (TB), and cryptococcal meningitis. Infectious encephalitis was considered less likely due to cranial nerve involvement and the CSF findings of very high protein and very low glucose. Cerebral malaria was also considered but thought unlikely in a semi-immune adult, and cranial nerve palsies are an unusual feature. Neither the clinical presentation nor the initial CSF results could reliably differentiate between the three main meningitis differentials.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was started on pragmatic treatment to cover bacterial, cryptococcal, and tuberculous meningitis; this included ceftriaxone 2g bid, fluconazole 1200mg od, and treatment for presumptive TB-meningitis. After the diagnosis was established by detection of acid-fast bacilli, she continued treatment. However, a few days into treatment, the patient slipped into a coma. An MRI scan of her brain revealed bilateral basal ganglia infarctions. She died in the hospital.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was tuberculous meningitis. This was established in a 26-year-old, HIV-reactive woman who presented with a subacute infectious meningitis syndrome characterized by headache, confusion, fever, and a left third cranial nerve palsy. The diagnosis was strongly supported by CSF findings of a markedly raised opening pressure (32cmH2O), very high protein (3.0 g/L), and very low glucose (1.3 mmol/L). The diagnosis was definitively confirmed by the detection of acid-fast bacilli in the CSF. The patient developed fatal complications, specifically bilateral basal ganglia infarctions, and died despite treatment.
